title: Ox forgotten
hook: seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man alone at ease

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sixth picture: the herdsman riding home on the ox, playing the flute, the struggle over. Your line: riding home.

The seventh picture has something missing. The herdsman is home, sitting outside a small thatched hut in the sun, rested, maybe half dozing. The whip and the rope lie idle, or hang on the wall. And the ox, the animal this whole series has been about, the one he searched for, tracked, glimpsed, caught, tamed and rode, is nowhere in the picture. He hasn't lost it. He's forgotten it.
screen: `HOME, OUTSIDE A THATCHED HUT.` → `WHIP AND ROPE LIE IDLE.` → `NO OX IN THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the ox was a way of speaking. The preface, in paraphrase, says the teaching is one, and the ox was only a temporary subject, something to point with. Like the moon coming out from behind the clouds, what was there all along is simply clear now. The ox was never a separate creature out in the hills. It was a picture for something the herdsman had all along. Second, a raft is for crossing. In an early sutta, the Buddha tells of a man who builds a raft to cross a river. Once across, he doesn't hoist it onto his head and carry it on, however useful it was. He leaves it at the shore. Teachings help you cross, the Buddha said; they aren't for clinging to. The seventh picture puts the raft down. Third, forgetting is not losing. When a skill becomes yours, you stop thinking about it. A practiced cook doesn't recite the recipe. A good friend doesn't keep a ledger. The ox is forgotten because there's nothing left to manage. Fourth, the man remains. The picture's full Chinese title says the ox is forgotten and the person remains. He's still there, at ease, someone who has finished a long job. Tomorrow even he drops out of the frame. Today the picture is restful: a quiet yard, a morning sun, tools hung up, nothing more to chase.
screen: `THE OX WAS A WAY OF SPEAKING.` · `A RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · `FORGETTING IS NOT LOSING.` · `THE OX GONE, THE MAN REMAINS.` · then, large: `THE OX FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Sit the way someone sits after finishing a long job, with no technique today: no counting the breath, no watching for wandering, no trying to be calm. If you catch yourself checking whether you're doing it right, set that down too. Just rest, the way the herdsman rests in the sun outside his hut.
Ox forgotten. The seventh oxherding picture: home and at ease, the herdsman no longer needs the ox, which was a way of pointing all along; the man remains. Today's word.
Your line: the ox forgotten. The raft is left at the shore, and nothing is lost. Rest well.

howItsDone: Some Zen teachers pair the seventh oxherding picture with the Buddha's parable of the raft to warn students against clinging even to their methods and to describe practice that no longer needs managing.

fork.setup: you've crossed the river on a raft you built yourself. it served you well. what does the Buddha's parable say to do with it?
options: carry it on your head, in gratitude.
leave it at the shore and go on.
burn it so no one else uses it.
fork.reveal: in the parable the raft is left at the shore: teachings are for crossing over, not for clinging to. the seventh picture puts the ox down the same way.

original.note: Chinese (wangniu cunren): 'the ox forgotten, the person remains', the name of the seventh oxherding picture.

what a scholar hears: the full title says the ox is forgotten and the person remains, setting up the eighth picture, where both drop away.

the poem often called faith in mind

chat.says: Why would the herdsman just forget the ox after all that work?
options: The ox was a way of pointing. Like a raft once you're across, it's not for carrying.
He got careless, and now the ox has wandered off into the hills again.
The ox never existed, so the whole long search was a waste of time.
chat.meaning: The preface calls the ox a temporary subject. Like the Buddha's raft, it helps you cross; forgetting it isn't losing it.

sutta.meaning: a discourse of the Buddha, in the early Pali texts

the Buddha.meaning: the awakened teacher who told the parable of the raft

oxherding picture.meaning: one of ten Zen pictures mapping practice as finding an ox
